summary: On June 8, 2011, World IPv6 Day, several key content providers offered both IPv4 and IPv6 services, and hundreds of organizations took part. The event went largely unnoticed by the public, which suggested no major problems. This informational document reports some measurements of the day from an end-user perspective.

eli5.summary: One day, big websites turned on the new internet addresses to test them. This reports how it looked from regular users' computers.

questions: what happened on world ipv6 day
how many websites had ipv6 in 2011
subtitle: How the Internet's big websites tested IPv6 on a single day in 2011.

tldr.problem: Major websites were hesitant to enable IPv6 because they feared unknown problems or failures. Before turning it on permanently, the industry wanted to test IPv6 at scale for a day.
tldr.mechanism: On June 8, 2011, hundreds of large content providers and organizations turned on IPv6 for 24 hours. Researchers measured how many websites offered IPv6, whether connections worked, and whether speeds were comparable to IPv4.
tldr.outcome: The event showed that roughly one third of the top 100 websites could offer IPv6, and when both protocols were available, delays and connection quality were nearly identical. The day spurred permanent adoption by some sites.

facts.label: IPv6 sites in top 100 during the event

today: RFC 6948 documents measurements from a pivotal moment in IPv6 adoption. The results showed that production-quality IPv6 networks were available and functional, paving the way for sustained IPv6 deployment. While the field has evolved substantially since 2011, the findings remain relevant as evidence that large-scale IPv6 deployment is feasible and that networks designed with IPv6 in mind can perform comparably to IPv4.

sections.title: Why Test IPv6
sections.content:
IPv6 is the new version of the Internet address system, created because IPv4 was running out of addresses. By 2011, large websites wanted to offer IPv6, but they worried about unknown problems. Some operators reported that attempting IPv6 sometimes made applications pause or fail as they waited for broken IPv6 connections to time out. The Web browsers, servers, and networks supporting IPv6 had not been tested at scale with real traffic from millions of users.

World IPv6 Day was organized to answer key questions: How many of the world's most visited websites would enable IPv6? Would their IPv6 networks work as well as IPv4? Would users experience problems or delays? By testing for just 24 hours, large networks could see what would happen without committing to permanent IPv6 deployment.
sections.eli5: People wanted to know if the new addressing system actually worked when millions of people tried it at once.

sections.title: How the Measurement Was Done
sections.content:
The researchers used the Alexa top 10,000 most popular websites and performed DNS queries to see which had both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. They tested multiple hostname variations (like www, www6, ipv6, and v6) to find all available addresses. For sites that had both address types, they then attempted TCP connections to port 80 (HTTP) on both IPv4 and IPv6 to measure connection success rates and setup delays.

Measurements started one week before the event (June 1) and continued through July 11, with tests running every three hours. Each test cycle took about two to two-and-a-half hours to complete. The researchers also measured the median delay difference between IPv4 and IPv6 connection setup to understand performance parity.
sections.eli5: Every three hours, they checked the top 10,000 websites to see which ones had new-style addresses and whether you could actually connect to them.

sections.title: IPv6 DNS Availability Spike
sections.content:
Before World IPv6 Day, only 245 of the top 10,000 websites (2.45%) had both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses published in the DNS. In the week leading up to the event, this number slowly increased to 306. When the event started on June 8 at UTC midnight, it jumped rapidly, peaking at 491 sites (4.91%) at 19:30 UTC that day. The results were even more dramatic for the top 100 most popular sites: only 14 had IPv6 before the day, and 36 had it during the day.

After the event ended, many sites removed their IPv6 addresses, but not all: the number stabilized at around 310 websites (over 3% of the 10,000), showing a permanent increase. For the commonly used 'www' hostname specifically, the number of AAAA records more than tripled during the day (from 116 to 374) and remained elevated afterward.
sections.eli5: On that one day, five times more websites suddenly had new-style addresses. Some turned them off afterward, but many kept them on.

sections.title: Connection Success and Performance
sections.content:
For IPv4, the baseline TCP connection failure rate was around 1 to 3% throughout the period. For IPv6, the initial failure rate was much higher (up to 25%), because many of the early IPv6 addresses were experimental or misconfigured. As the event approached and participating sites prepared their networks, the IPv6 failure rate dropped to about 20%. During World IPv6 Day itself, as large professional networks came online, the failure rate fell to just above 10%, and remained at 15 to 20% afterward.

When comparing connection delays between IPv4 and IPv6, the median delay difference stayed within 3 milliseconds of zero for most of the period, showing that the two protocols performed almost identically. Even the mean delay difference, which is more sensitive to outliers, remained within plus or minus 5 milliseconds most of the time. Sites with poor IPv6 connectivity or multiple packet retransmissions created occasional spikes, but production-quality IPv6 networks showed performance matching IPv4.
sections.eli5: When both addresses worked, the new-style ones were just as fast as the old ones. Some early test addresses failed, but that improved as sites got ready.

sections.title: Lessons and Impact
sections.content:
World IPv6 Day demonstrated that the Internet infrastructure was ready for IPv6. One of the most important findings was that a large fraction of the top 100 websites could enable IPv6 with production-quality networks. The event showed that the three to four percent permanent increase in IPv6-capable websites afterward came from the exercise itself; some organizations that had not planned permanent IPv6 deployment were inspired by the day's success to keep their IPv6 networks running.

The measurements also revealed shortcomings: initial IPv6 configurations often had errors, such as localhost addresses or link-local addresses being published in DNS. Nevertheless, the conclusion was clear that if a small number of the world's most popular websites offer IPv6, the traffic volume they represent is large enough to substantially change Internet usage patterns. The key remaining challenge identified was not technology but deployment: enabling IPv6 in the access networks that serve end users.
sections.eli5: The test proved that big websites and networks could handle new-style addresses reliably. The next job was to turn it on everywhere, not just for a day.
